feedback.reason: Old v1 clients coexist with the new index, so preserve their observable contract while introducing the cursor version. Retire offset only after measured adoption and a defined support boundary.
feedback.details: Keep v1 behavior stable for existing readers, and add an explicit v2 cursor contract with query binding and index watermark. Run both during the migration window, observe client usage and correctness, and document the retirement condition. A server-side version adapter may be used, but returning only cursor fields to v1 readers breaks them. Compatibility should be evidence-based, not permanent by default.

messages.text: Old clients still send offset requests and cannot continue pagination after the one-sided cutover.
Adding a response field does not preserve the old request/response behavior if offset stops working.
This avoids an immediate break but leaves permanent ambiguous support and operational cost.
A cursor bound to no index view may continue against different membership/order and hide lag.

options.text: Keep v1 offset behavior; add a versioned cursor contract with watermark and dual support during migration.
Deploy cursor-only responses immediately and require every client to upgrade in the same release.
Add a cursor field to the v1 response and assume old clients will ignore it while the server stops honoring offset.
Keep both contracts indefinitely without tracking adoption or defining a retirement date.
Return a cursor without its index version/watermark and assume clients can continue across index rebuilds.

prompt: Search API v1 accepts offset=100. A new index supports opaque search-after cursors and returns a source/index watermark. Old mobile clients remain active for a month. How should the API evolve without breaking those readers?

feedback.reason: Both reader behaviors are explicit: old clients ignore unknown optional fields and new clients tolerate absence. An additive optional field with a documented default preserves both directions of coexistence.
feedback.details: Define what missing confidence means, deploy readers that accept the field when present and absent, then allow writers to populate it. Leave duration’s existing meaning untouched. Validate old-reader behavior with the actual v1 contract. Additive syntax alone is not enough when readers reject unknown fields or new readers assume the field always exists.

messages.text: Old clients may reject an unknown required field, so the rollout depends on a coordinated upgrade that is unavailable.
Old readers still interpret duration as time, so changing its meaning corrupts their result.
Old payloads omit the value during coexistence, so the new reader fails its own compatibility window.
Indefinite duplicate fields create conflicting sources of truth instead of a staged optional migration.

options.text: Add optional etaConfidence with a documented default; keep old response fields and readers valid.
Make etaConfidence required and deploy writers that always send it before old readers are upgraded.
Reuse duration as the confidence value and document the changed interpretation for new clients.
Deploy new readers that require etaConfidence before any writer sends the optional field.
Add etaConfidenceV2 and keep multiple confidence fields forever without deciding which is authoritative.

prompt: Route planning response v1 contains routeId and duration. V2 adds optional etaConfidence; old readers ignore unknown optional fields and new readers default the field when absent. No coordinated deployment is possible. What migration is safest?

feedback.reason: A boolean false is terminal to the old reader, while a timeout does not prove the provider declined the charge. A nonterminal 503 with a status Location lets v1 resolve the same paymentIntentId without launching another charge.
feedback.details: Persist paymentIntentId and the provider request before calling the provider. For an unknown response, return the specified nonterminal 503 plus status Location and hold the original intent; do not report false or create a second charge until reconciliation establishes the result. V2 may represent PENDING/UNKNOWN directly. A retry must query or resume the same stable intent, not create a new one.

messages.text: Encoding unknown as false triggers the legacy reader’s retry path; it may create another charge for the unresolved paymentIntentId.
Unversioned values do not solve v1’s false-as-final behavior; retain the v1 status-location path and expose new states through the staged v2 contract.
A timeout is ambiguous, not proof of no charge; false would collapse unknown into failure.
A client-side cache cannot establish provider state and leaves the server contract unable to express uncertainty.

options.text: Keep one paymentIntentId and return nonterminal 503 plus status Location until reconciliation; never start a fresh charge.
Encode PENDING and UNKNOWN as false in v1 and let the client decide whether to retry.
Add new enum values to the existing v1 response and assume every old client tolerates unknown values.
Set status=false whenever the provider response times out, even if authorization may have completed.
Keep only the boolean forever and handle pending outcomes in an unrelated client cache.

prompt: Payment API v1 returns a boolean and requires a stable paymentIntentId that can be queried at a status location. A provider timeout can leave the charge outcome unknown; v2 needs PENDING and UNKNOWN. V1 readers treat false as final failure and submit another charge. What compatibility behavior can prevent a duplicate charge?

feedback.reason: Absent v1 priority is ambiguous and cannot safely mean low. Establish an explicit conservative fallback, deploy tolerant readers, then migrate producers with evidence before retiring v1.
feedback.details: Version the envelope or add an optional priority with a documented rule for absence. The consumer must safely route or quarantine legacy cases rather than silently demoting them. Upgrade producers, measure which versions still omit the field, and remove the fallback only after coverage is proven. A required field is only safe after old producers are retired.

messages.text: A v1 producer may be sending a high-risk case; the default silently violates its required handling.
Legacy producers remain active, so an immediate hard cutover loses cases during coexistence.
Heuristic parsing can misclassify a high-risk case and gives no consistent migration contract.
Compatibility parsing alone does not preserve the priority behavior the new field was introduced to express.

options.text: Define a safe absent-priority rule and upgrade readers before producers; quarantine ambiguous high-risk legacy cases.
Default an absent priority to low so legacy messages enter the ordinary queue without delaying.
Reject every v1 envelope as soon as the new consumer launches, without a producer transition window.
Infer priority from arbitrary payload text with no stable schema or audited mapping.
Accept both schemas but route all cases through one FIFO queue regardless of the new field.

prompt: Fraud envelope v1 has caseId and payload. V2 adds priority, but some v1 producers omit it and may send high-risk cases during rollout. The queue must not silently route them as low priority. What compatibility rule should govern migration?

feedback.reason: Historical downloads are immutable artifacts with established units and grouping. Version the new representation and keep old export IDs bound to their original bytes and provenance.
feedback.details: Retain each v1 artifact with its snapshot, rules revision, and schema version. New v2 exports receive an explicit version and new identity; any conversion must state how decimal dollars map to integer minor units and how rows regroup. A retry of an old export returns its original artifact. Updating the serializer in place breaks audit reproducibility.

messages.text: Old readers would misread units, and the archived v1 artifact would no longer preserve its original meaning.
A retry would return different bytes under the same historical identity.
The same request identity would have ambiguous schema and amount units.
Without provenance, auditors cannot reproduce or interpret the original v1 output.

options.text: Keep v1 exports immutable and version v2 amount units and row shape under a new export contract.
Change the meaning of amount in place and let existing v1 readers interpret the new integer as dollars.
Recalculate any old export ID using the current v2 grouping and amount representation.
Return either v1 or v2 rows from the same endpoint based on whichever backend is available.
Rewrite historical exports to v2 and discard the original rules/snapshot metadata.

prompt: Payroll export v1 stores amount as decimal dollars. V2 stores integer minor units and changes row grouping. A user may download an old v1 export years later by its export ID. How should the migration preserve audit meaning?

feedback.reason: A numeric value is not interpretable without its unit and currency. Version the changed representation and preserve v1 semantics until old readers are safely retired.
feedback.details: Expose integer minor units with an explicit currency code in a versioned field or endpoint. During coexistence, keep the existing decimal field’s semantics unchanged and document any conversion rounding. Track reader adoption before removing v1. Renaming or changing the unit without a version makes syntactically valid values economically wrong.

messages.text: Old readers will parse cents as whole currency units and misreport the amount.
Old clients can reject the new required shape or still depend on the old field.
Currency is part of the value’s meaning and cannot be safely inferred from presentation settings.
Readers can disagree about which value to trust, leaving a permanent contract ambiguity.

options.text: Add a versioned amount representation with explicit currency and minor-unit meaning.
Change the existing total field from decimal units to integer cents without changing its name or version.
Add a required cents field to the current response and stop returning the old decimal field immediately.
Send the integer total but infer currency from locale or a client preference.
Return both decimal and minor-unit fields indefinitely without specifying which is canonical.

prompt: A financial API v1 returns totals as decimal currency units. V2 needs integer minor units and explicit currency; some readers still parse the v1 decimal field. How should the schema evolve?

feedback.reason: Optional metadata is compatible only if absence and unknown-field behavior are defined at both reader generations. Test the old/new directions and avoid inventing values for historical events.
feedback.details: Specify the semantics when deviceMetadata is absent, then test v1 producer→new consumer and v2 producer→old consumer with real serializers. Add the field without changing existing event meaning. Backfill only when the source contains authoritative metadata; otherwise retain absence. A staged producer rollout can begin after readers tolerate both forms.

messages.text: Old producers remain active, so the new consumer would reject valid messages during coexistence.
The assumption is unverified; old consumer behavior is a compatibility fact to test, not infer from additive syntax.
Guessed backfill invents source facts and can corrupt analytics.
The rollout still includes v1 producers, so a required field breaks legitimate old writes.

options.text: Make deviceMetadata optional with defined absence semantics for old producers and consumers.
Deploy new consumers that reject v1 events without deviceMetadata.
Send the field to old consumers without checking whether their deserializers reject unknown properties.
Populate missing historical metadata with a guessed device value so every old event appears complete.
Make deviceMetadata required for all producers before old producers have a migration path.

prompt: Telemetry event v1 has deviceId and eventTime. V2 adds optional deviceMetadata. Old producers remain active, and new consumers must accept v1 events; during rollout, old consumers may receive v2 events. What compatibility tests and field rule are needed?

feedback.reason: Mapping pending to false triggers old callers to create another delivery; mapping it to true falsely claims provider success. A stable delivery identity and a nonterminal resolution path avoid both errors.
feedback.details: Keep one deliveryId for the notification across retries. New readers can use RETRY_PENDING; old readers need a documented nonterminal response and status location so they can query the same delivery rather than resubmit it as new. Do not claim delivered before provider acceptance or convert an in-progress delivery to terminal failure. If an old request cannot be matched to a stable deliveryId, fail closed without creating another provider delivery; do not guess that the old request is new.

messages.text: Old clients interpret false as final failure and may create a second notification while the original is retrying.
The described readers do not have that behavior; unversioned expansion may trigger unsafe retry logic.
That falsely claims the provider delivered the notification before confirmation.
Local state cannot reconcile the sender and provider. If a legacy request cannot be matched to a stable deliveryId, fail closed rather than create another delivery.

options.text: Expose RETRY_PENDING through a staged contract and resolve old-client retries against the same delivery ID.
Map RETRY_PENDING to delivered=false in v1 and let old clients submit a new delivery.
Add RETRY_PENDING to v1 and assume old clients will handle the unknown status safely.
Map RETRY_PENDING to delivered=true so old clients do not retry.
Keep the server boolean unchanged and store pending state only in the current client’s local cache.

prompt: Notification delivery v1 has a stable deliveryId and status location. V2 must expose RETRY_PENDING without claiming provider success. Old clients treat false as terminal failure and immediately resend. How should the migration prevent duplicate delivery?

feedback.reason: The actor field is evidence, not decoration. Require authenticated attribution for new events and preserve honest unknown status for legacy records unless authoritative evidence supports migration.
feedback.details: Introduce a versioned event contract with server-bound principal identity for new appends. Keep readers able to interpret legacy events with an explicit unknown actor state. Migrate historical rows only when trusted audit evidence maps them to a principal; never fill gaps with a guessed service account. Retire old writers after observed adoption and a documented transition.

messages.text: A default would fabricate attribution for actions whose actor is unknown.
Old producers/readers coexist and a hard cutover can lose valid in-flight audit history.
Presence is not provenance; the authenticated principal must be bound to the event.
This does not establish the new attribution requirement or provide a retirement condition.

options.text: Require authenticated actor IDs for new writes; reject ambiguous legacy events without fabricating history.
Rewrite every historical missing actor as “system” so the new mandatory field is populated.
Reject every legacy event and reader immediately because new records require an actor ID.
Make actorId mandatory in the payload but trust whatever identifier an unauthenticated client supplies.
Keep actor optional for all new events and never measure whether old producers have migrated.

prompt: An audit event is changing from optional actor metadata to a mandatory authenticated actor identifier. Historical records may lack that identity, and the source cannot prove who performed some actions. What schema migration is defensible?

feedback.reason: A revisionless delivery has no ordering evidence, so neither arrival time nor a default value can prove it is newer. Quarantine it until its authoritative revision can be verified.
feedback.details: Keep the current shipment state unchanged for any revisionless event during migration. Upgrade producers to include stable event IDs and an authoritative monotonic shipmentRevision, verify all active writers provide it, then make receiver validation mandatory. A quarantined event can be replayed only after its source order is established; deduplication handles repeated identity but does not establish order.

messages.text: This rejects legacy traffic without first preserving it in a quarantine/replay path; it can lose updates during the overlap.
Assigning revision zero is unsafe, and accepting the event can overwrite current state; quarantine it instead.
Arrival time is not source order, so a delayed old update can overwrite the latest shipment state.
Deduplication suppresses a repeated event ID but provides no ordering proof for a distinct revisionless event.

options.text: Quarantine revisionless carrier events until a verifiable source revision is supplied and coverage is proven.
This rejects legacy traffic without first preserving it in a quarantine/replay path; it can lose updates during the overlap.
Assigning revision zero is unsafe, and accepting the event can overwrite current state; quarantine it instead.
Arrival time is not source order, so a delayed old update can overwrite the latest shipment state.
Deduplication suppresses a repeated event ID but provides no ordering proof for a distinct revisionless event.

prompt: Carrier producers are gradually adding shipmentRevision. Old and new producers may overlap, deliveries can be duplicated or delayed, and revision will become required for monotonic state enforcement. Until every producer sends a verifiable revision, how must the receiver handle a revisionless delivery so it cannot overwrite current shipment state?

feedback.reason: Without stable identity, the service cannot tell a retry from a new extraction. Calling the billable provider again could charge twice, so the ambiguous attempt must remain unresolved until the same intent is identified.
feedback.details: For v2, persist operationId and its request parameters before the provider call, return the existing job for an identical retry, and reject reuse with changed parameters. For a legacy timeout or retry whose intent cannot be matched, return/retain UNKNOWN or reject it without another billable side effect; do not guess identity from file content or create a fresh job. Track legacy usage, provide a bounded migration window, and require stable operationId before further billable execution.

messages.text: A new job ID makes an ambiguous retry look like a new intent and can cause a second provider charge.
File equality does not identify the requested operation; deduplicating by content can suppress a legitimate new extraction and still cannot resolve an unknown prior charge.
An immediate global cutoff is not a measured migration; preserve non-billable status access and move callers to stable operation IDs on a bounded schedule.
An unbound or changed operationId cannot identify the original billable intent; persist and compare request parameters before replay.

options.text: Hold unmatched legacy retries UNKNOWN without a provider call; require a stable operationId before billable execution.
A new job ID makes an ambiguous retry look like a new intent and can cause a second provider charge.
File equality does not identify the requested operation; deduplicating by content can suppress a legitimate new extraction and still cannot resolve an unknown prior charge.
An immediate global cutoff is not a measured migration; preserve non-billable status access and move callers to stable operation IDs on a bounded schedule.
An unbound or changed operationId cannot identify the original billable intent; persist and compare request parameters before replay.

prompt: An extraction API v1 may retry by creating a new job ID, and some active legacy callers provide no stable intent identity. V2 adds durable operationId so retries can resolve the same billable intent. During migration, what must happen to an ambiguous legacy retry before the service can safely make another billable provider call?

feedback.reason: The v1 boolean-like terminal states cannot represent uncertainty. Reporting failed can cause the client to reserve a second seat, so preserve and resolve the original intent through status lookup.
feedback.details: Persist the allocation intent before contacting the inventory authority. For an unknown response, return the established nonterminal/status-location behavior to v1 and let v2 expose pending/unknown explicitly. Repeated requests must resolve the original intent; only a confirmed final failure permits a new allocation. Keep the legacy response mapping until old clients are migrated. If an old request cannot be matched to its stable allocation intent, fail closed and hold it for reconciliation; do not allocate a new seat under a guessed identity.

messages.text: The seat may already be reserved; mapping unknown to failure can allocate a second ticket.
Queue acceptance is not a completed reservation and can produce a false ticket confirmation.
Old clients may reject new values or treat them as failure and trigger duplicate allocation.
Client-local state cannot query the inventory authority. If the request cannot be matched to its stable allocation ID, hold/fail closed instead of creating a second allocation.

options.text: Keep an unknown allocation under one stable intent and status location; never map it to terminal failure.
Map every timeout to failed in v1 and ask the old client to retry with a new request.
Return allocated as soon as the request is accepted into a queue, before the seat claim commits.
Add pending and unknown to the v1 enum without testing old client behavior.
Keep only the two-state server response and store pending locally on whichever client submitted the request.

prompt: Ticket API v1 requests carry a stable allocation intent ID that can be queried at a status location. V1 exposes only allocated or failed, and old clients retry when they see failed. A timeout may leave the seat outcome unknown; v2 needs pending, succeeded, and failed. How should an unmatched or unresolved request behave?

feedback.reason: Tenant scope is a security boundary. Versioning can stage client compatibility, but a legacy request without provable scope must fail closed rather than receive a permissive default.
feedback.details: Derive tenant authorization from the authenticated identity on the server and check it before querying. Add a v2 contract or access gate for clients that supply valid authenticated context. For legacy callers, either a trusted server-side mapping exists or the request is denied; do not trust a client tenant field. Measure and migrate callers, then retire the old route.

messages.text: A permissive default can resolve another tenant’s cases and violates server-side ownership.
An untrusted request field does not establish authorization for that tenant.
Unauthorized records have already been read and may reach logs or caches before filtering.
This may break active clients; safe migration should preserve service only when tenant scope can be proven.

options.text: Derive tenant scope from authenticated identity and version-gate clients that omit it.
Map a missing tenant to a shared default scope so v1 requests continue to return results.
Accept a tenantId supplied by the legacy client without checking it against authenticated identity.
Run the global search for v1 and filter returned cases by tenant after the query.
Remove v1 immediately without staging clients or a version/access transition.

prompt: Support search v1 accepts a caseId without tenant context. V2 must derive tenant from authenticated identity and reject requests missing that scope. Legacy clients are still deployed; permissive defaulting would expose another tenant’s cases. What migration is safe?

feedback.reason: The existing wire contract already distinguishes confirmed absence (404) from temporary source failure (503); preserve those meanings while adding freshness information to successful responses.
feedback.details: Keep 404 for a confirmed missing asset and 503 for a temporarily unavailable source. For a returned record, add optional status and as-of fields so v2 readers can identify stale projection data; define how a new reader interprets an absent field as the v1 result, and let old readers ignore the optional fields. Verify both reader generations without converting stale data into confirmed absence or outage.

messages.text: A shared empty response erases the existing difference between 404 confirmed absence and 503 temporary failure, and still hides projection staleness.
Replacing established responses immediately can break old readers and changes the known 404/503 wire meanings.
Treating stale projection as confirmed absence misleads clients and changes the meaning of the existing 404.
Without a documented absent-field default, a new reader cannot safely interpret old responses during rollout.

options.text: Preserve 404 for missing and 503 for unavailable; add optional stale/as-of metadata to successful results.
A shared empty response erases the existing difference between 404 confirmed absence and 503 temporary failure, and still hides projection staleness.
Replacing established responses immediately can break old readers and changes the known 404/503 wire meanings.
Treating stale projection as confirmed absence misleads clients and changes the meaning of the existing 404.
Without a documented absent-field default, a new reader cannot safely interpret old responses during rollout.

prompt: Media metadata v1 returns a record for success, HTTP 404 for confirmed absence, and HTTP 503 when the source is temporarily unavailable. V2 must also expose stale projection status and as-of time. Old readers tolerate optional response fields, and new readers can map an absent status to the old result. How should the contract evolve without changing the established 404/503 behavior?

feedback.reason: The replay guarantee is enforced at the physical effect boundary, and old firmware lacks that capability. Stage rollout by verified device capability instead of assuming the gateway or wire format is enough.
feedback.details: Upgrade gateways to understand both contracts, then deploy firmware that persists command identity/sequence and rejects already-applied commands. Route replay-sensitive commands only when the target device’s capability is known; otherwise use a safe legacy policy or reject/defer. Measure firmware coverage before making v2 mandatory. A gateway-only dedup table cannot resolve a device crash after actuation but before its response.

messages.text: The old device may reject the message or execute duplicates because it lacks the new replay guard.
The physical effect boundary must also know whether it already acted; gateway delivery records cannot prove device execution.
A constant sequence cannot distinguish a new command from a replay.
The migration lacks evidence that all devices can accept v2 and may interrupt valid control operations.

options.text: Stage gateway and device support for command sequence IDs; block unsafe execution on legacy firmware.
Start emitting sequence fields to every device immediately and assume old firmware will ignore unknown fields safely.
Deduplicate at the gateway and declare unsafe replay solved even though the device may execute twice after reconnect.
Assign sequence zero to old firmware commands and let that value authorize repeated actions.
Disable every v1 device immediately without a staged coverage check or fallback.

prompt: IoT command v2 adds command sequence and idempotency identity so devices can reject replay. Gateway readers update before firmware; many devices remain on v1 during rollout. Unsafe repeated actuation must be prevented. What transition policy is required?

feedback.reason: A stable delivery identity is useful only when the receiver understands and durably enforces it. Because some v1 parsers reject unknown fields, introduce the envelope through a staged, explicit compatibility boundary.
feedback.details: Negotiate receiver capability or use an explicit v2 envelope while preserving v1 bytes for old endpoints. Keep one deliveryId across retries and vary attempt metadata separately. Verify upgraded receivers persist dedup state before executing the side effect. Track receiver adoption and retire v1 through a defined policy; do not assume unknown fields are ignored.

messages.text: The prompt says some receivers reject unknown fields, so immediate expansion breaks them.
Attempts for one logical event need the same identity; fresh IDs bypass deduplication.
A parsed ID alone does not prevent duplicate processing unless the receiver enforces it durably.
Permanent untracked variants leave senders unable to know which duplicate-safety contract a receiver supports.

options.text: Add deliveryId and attempt metadata through a compatible payload version; deduplicate by stable identity.
Add deliveryId and attempt to every payload immediately and assume all v1 receivers ignore unknown properties.
Generate a new deliveryId for each attempt so receivers can identify individual sends.
Send the v2 field but do not verify that the receiver persists it before its side effect.
Keep two subtly different payloads indefinitely with no receiver capability registry or retirement rule.

prompt: Webhook payload v1 has event type and body. V2 adds stable deliveryId and attempt metadata for receiver deduplication. Some receivers reject unknown fields, so payload compatibility must be staged. What migration is safe?
